These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.

- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there.    **Pass `--pr` on any park a pull request or an issue would end**, not only on an
   approval, where it is required. It stamps `Ends-when: #<n> closed` on the item, and
   that is what makes the park end by itself: the janitor closes the item `done` when
   the target merges and `rejected` when it is closed unmerged. Without it the park
   stands until a person happens to read it.

   **A marked issue needs no write-back at all**: it is the item, so the approval
   park it wears *is* the in-review state and the failure park *is* the report (which
   is why `--pr` is still required on an approval — a park nobody can act on is not
   a park). The standing status is also what stops the next scheduler run adopting
   the same issue again; clearing it is a person's decision, made after reading what
   the run said. Only an item filed under the older shadow model writes back to a
   different issue, and the command does that too.

   Only `task:status:needs-human-failure` (and a park whose kind cannot be decoded) holds the
   task's lane — while one is open the generator files no further occurrence of
   this task. The other three wait for their human while the schedule carries on,
   so leaving one open costs nobody but the person it names.

   The `claudinite-task-exec` record goes onto the item, in the same comment, and
   the command writes it — Actions logs expire and the item does not, so the item
   is where a record has to live. Nothing here is yours to print by hand.

7. **Capture this session before you end it.** Last step, after the item is
   converged, and run it whichever way step 6 went:

   ```bash
   CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE=<n> node <engine>/hooks/session-end-command.mjs
   ```

   That runner invokes whatever session-end steps this repo's declared packs
   contribute; it knows nothing about what any of them do, and a repo that
   contributes none does nothing. Nobody is sitting in front of this session, so it
   ends by having its container reclaimed — precisely the ending that fires no
   `SessionEnd` hook. Left to the hook, every unattended run would leave no record
   of itself anywhere: not of the skills it loaded, not of the checks that caught
   something, not of how the work actually went, and not of the record you just
   printed. `CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE` is what files those logs under the item that
   ran, rather than under nothing.

   It cannot fail your run — the item is already converged and this changes nothing
   on GitHub. If it reports an error, **say so plainly in your final message** and
   end anyway.

## The one standing bound

You execute **this one item and nothing else**. Never list other work items,
never sweep the queue, never act on a second issue in this session — however
obviously stuck another one looks. Recovery is code that runs elsewhere, and a
session that helps out is how one item becomes three duplicate PRs.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

1	---
2	name: prose-to-checks
3	description: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
4	---
5	
6	# Convert existing prose to checks
7	
8	A completeness-critic over a repo's own packs: prose that is always-testable but was never converted
9	becomes a check, so the packs keep shedding context over time instead of only at the moment a rule is
10	first learned.
11	
12	## Two callers, differing only in scope
13	
14	- **The upgrade pass**, as the last step of a
15	  [growth-extract](../../tasks/growth-extract/task.md) run: the scope is the prose **that run just
16	  wrote**. Extraction already descends the promotion ladder per lesson, but a lesson written as prose
17	  under time pressure is exactly where a convertible rule hides, so it gets asked once more before the
18	  PR opens. Never widen from here into the standing backlog.
19	- **The weekly [prose-to-checks-sweep](../../tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)**: the scope is the
20	  **standing backlog** — everything under the pack paths configured for this repo, which the task
21	  passes in its Context. A consuming repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`) by
22	  default — projects don't improve core canon packs — while **Claudinite itself** also sweeps its core
23	  `packs/`. Read the prose under those paths (each pack's `RULES.md`, and any `SKILL.md` beside them).
24	
25	Plus on demand, when someone asks. Either way: never edit a read-only mounted canon pack under
26	`.claudinite/shared/`. Everything below is identical for both callers.
27	
28	## First gate — a working rule, not a product statement
29	
30	Before asking whether a rule is *testable*, ask whether it belongs to a pack at all: **does it govern
31	how we work, or state what the product does?** A pack — canon or local — homes the conventions,
32	gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks whatever the feature happens to be. A rule
33	asserting which entities exist, what a surface must render, or that a feature's parts are wired to
34	each other is a **requirement**; its home is the project's executable spec and the suite that proves
35	it.
36	
37	This gate comes **first** because product statements sail through the check-the-world test below —
38	"this module must export `X`" has an obvious static signature. Converting one splits a feature's
39	definition across two systems and lands half of it in the one no test of the product ever reads.
40	Load-bearingness is not the test: a real gap in product coverage is a *requirements* gap. Neither is build
41	quality — a product statement converts into a genuinely well-made check, clean parse and see-it-fail proof and
42	all, and is still the wrong kind. The discriminator, applied **before** you write anything: *if the product
43	changed its mind tomorrow, would this rule be wrong?* Wrong → it's a requirement, and a red check would report
44	a product decision as a process violation. Still true whatever the product decides → it's a working rule.
45	
46	A product statement already sitting in pack prose is mis-homed, and a sweep is not the place to
47	re-home it. **Leave the prose and log it** as a mis-homed rule, the same way an un-checkable
48	candidate is logged — never cement it as a check.
49	
50	## What to look for — the check-the-world test
51	
52	For each rule that cleared the gate, ask the one question from
53	[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
54	signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**
55	
56	- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
57	  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
58	- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
59	  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
60	  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.
61	
62	**"Already covered by another check" is a claim to test, not to reason out** — hand the sibling check a file
63	that violates the rule before dropping the candidate as a duplicate. A ban list only covers the routes whoever
64	wrote it thought of, so the routes it misses are invisible to exactly the reasoning that drew it: three sweeps
65	running dropped an "the app opens no socket" rule because a neighbouring check banned the obvious networking
66	import, while the base library re-exported a raw socket call that sailed straight through.
67	
68	**"Not statically checkable" is a verdict about the tree's shape when it was taken, not about the rule —
69	re-derive it against today's sources.** A removal, a migration or a consolidation can collapse the entry points
70	a rule had to cover, and the objection dies with them: a "one deletable storage directory" rule needed
71	data-flow tracing while many entry points wrote paths, and needed none once one root remained. So when a sweep
72	meets prose an earlier sweep left behind, re-ask the question rather than trusting the recorded answer. (This
73	covers the *technical* verdict only — an owner's rejection of a conversion is settled.)
74	
75	**Read the conversion tracker's prior comments before authoring, not after.** Independent re-derivation is
76	exactly how duplicate work happens: a fresh reading of the same prose will happily re-nominate a rule, build it
77	out in full, and only then discover it was built and rejected before. The tracker is a precondition of the
78	work, not a place to log it — and record each rejection with its reason so the next run can act on it.
79	
80	**A static signature is necessary, not sufficient.** Both shapes the working-discipline rules bar
81	— a rule that pins today's code in place, and one derivable from the product's requirements —
82	answer *yes* here, so screen every candidate against that bar before converting it. Leave either
83	where it is; routing a requirement to the spec and its suite is its own change, not this sweep's.
84	
85	The check-the-world rule from DESIGN holds: if a rule is always-testable, it was never really
86	part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.
87	
88	## How to convert one
89	
90	Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
91	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:
92	
93	> **The upgrade-pass caller lands inside growth-extract's own PR**, which auto-merges after CI — so the
94	> see-it-fail fixture is the only gate a converted check gets there. Convert only what you can prove;
95	> anything shakier stays prose and waits for the weekly sweep's reviewed PR.
96	
97	1. **Author the check** in the owning pack, at the ladder's highest check rung the rule allows: an entry
98	   in `<pack>/declared-checks.json` when its logic is patterns over files, dropping to `<pack>/<rule>.mjs`
99	   listed in `pack.mjs` only when it needs what patterns can't say. Either way the failure message *is*
100	   the rule (what / why / fix — plus, for a rule module, the `doc:` pointer back to the prose; a
101	   declaration carries no pointer and must state its own case).
102	2. **Write the fixture first and see it fail** — a violating fixture must find, a clean one must
103	   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
104	   doesn't ship.
105	3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory when the rule is
106	   directional by kind, or when the condition is blocking-grade but **irreversible by the time it is
107	   observable** (an append-only transcript, a published artifact). A blocking finding no edit can
108	   retract never converges — it spends every remaining Stop cycle on something nothing can fix.
109	   Advisory there is *diagnostic*: it names the cause the moment it appears.
110	   - **Declare `since: '<today>'` beside the severity.** A blocking check is enforced as advisory for
111	     its first two weeks, so a conversion whose backlog the tree still carries lands at its real
112	     severity now and starts biting once somebody has had time to clear it. Never soften a real
113	     defect to `advisory` for that reason — the window is what makes softening unnecessary.
114	   - **Prefer a positive allowlist over an enumerated list of the bad cases.** Match the one allowed
115	     shape and flag everything else, rather than banning the violations you can name. An allowlist
116	     catches a variant that doesn't exist yet the day it lands, and turns an indirection (a value
117	     passed through a variable instead of written literally) into a finding too — refusing to reason
118	     about indirection is the feature. Invert only where the allowed set is genuinely open-ended.
119	4. **Delete the prose the check now covers** — whole, never trimmed. The deletion test below is
120	   how you decide which paragraphs those are.
121	
122	**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
123	its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
124	which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's
125	*own* header list, not elsewhere in the template.) Parse only as much as you need, and hold the
126	check to the same fixture bar.
127	
128	**When a rule mandates a *form*, the check asserts that form — never the intent behind it.** Where
129	the prose says *write it exactly like this*, the check's whole job is deciding whether the artifact
130	is that form; inferring what the author meant is unbounded in the wrong direction and leaves the

---
name: prose-to-checks
description: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
---

# Convert existing prose to checks

A completeness-critic over a repo's own packs: prose that is always-testable but was never converted
becomes a check, so the packs keep shedding context over time instead of only at the moment a rule is
first learned.

## Two callers, differing only in scope

- **The upgrade pass**, as the last step of a
  [growth-extract](../../tasks/growth-extract/task.md) run: the scope is the prose **that run just
  wrote**. Extraction already descends the promotion ladder per lesson, but a lesson written as prose
  under time pressure is exactly where a convertible rule hides, so it gets asked once more before the
  PR opens. Never widen from here into the standing backlog.
- **The weekly [prose-to-checks-sweep](../../tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)**: the scope is the
  **standing backlog** — everything under the pack paths configured for this repo, which the task
  passes in its Context. A consuming repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`) by
  default — projects don't improve core canon packs — while **Claudinite itself** also sweeps its core
  `packs/`. Read the prose under those paths (each pack's `RULES.md`, and any `SKILL.md` beside them).

Plus on demand, when someone asks. Either way: never edit a read-only mounted canon pack under
`.claudinite/shared/`. Everything below is identical for both callers.

## First gate — a working rule, not a product statement

Before asking whether a rule is *testable*, ask whether it belongs to a pack at all: **does it govern
how we work, or state what the product does?** A pack — canon or local — homes the conventions,
gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks whatever the feature happens to be. A rule
asserting which entities exist, what a surface must render, or that a feature's parts are wired to
each other is a **requirement**; its home is the project's executable spec and the suite that proves
it.

This gate comes **first** because product statements sail through the check-the-world test below —
"this module must export `X`" has an obvious static signature. Converting one splits a feature's
definition across two systems and lands half of it in the one no test of the product ever reads.
Load-bearingness is not the test: a real gap in product coverage is a *requirements* gap. Neither is build
quality — a product statement converts into a genuinely well-made check, clean parse and see-it-fail proof and
all, and is still the wrong kind. The discriminator, applied **before** you write anything: *if the product
changed its mind tomorrow, would this rule be wrong?* Wrong → it's a requirement, and a red check would report
a product decision as a process violation. Still true whatever the product decides → it's a working rule.

A product statement already sitting in pack prose is mis-homed, and a sweep is not the place to
re-home it. **Leave the prose and log it** as a mis-homed rule, the same way an un-checkable
candidate is logged — never cement it as a check.

## What to look for — the check-the-world test

For each rule that cleared the gate, ask the one question from
[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**

- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.

**"Already covered by another check" is a claim to test, not to reason out** — hand the sibling check a file
that violates the rule before dropping the candidate as a duplicate. A ban list only covers the routes whoever
wrote it thought of, so the routes it misses are invisible to exactly the reasoning that drew it: three sweeps
running dropped an "the app opens no socket" rule because a neighbouring check banned the obvious networking
import, while the base library re-exported a raw socket call that sailed straight through.

**"Not statically checkable" is a verdict about the tree's shape when it was taken, not about the rule —
re-derive it against today's sources.** A removal, a migration or a consolidation can collapse the entry points
a rule had to cover, and the objection dies with them: a "one deletable storage directory" rule needed
data-flow tracing while many entry points wrote paths, and needed none once one root remained. So when a sweep
meets prose an earlier sweep left behind, re-ask the question rather than trusting the recorded answer. (This
covers the *technical* verdict only — an owner's rejection of a conversion is settled.)

**Read the conversion tracker's prior comments before authoring, not after.** Independent re-derivation is
exactly how duplicate work happens: a fresh reading of the same prose will happily re-nominate a rule, build it
out in full, and only then discover it was built and rejected before. The tracker is a precondition of the
work, not a place to log it — and record each rejection with its reason so the next run can act on it.

**A static signature is necessary, not sufficient.** Both shapes the working-discipline rules bar
— a rule that pins today's code in place, and one derivable from the product's requirements —
answer *yes* here, so screen every candidate against that bar before converting it. Leave either
where it is; routing a requirement to the spec and its suite is its own change, not this sweep's.

The check-the-world rule from DESIGN holds: if a rule is always-testable, it was never really
part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.

## How to convert one

Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:

> **The upgrade-pass caller lands inside growth-extract's own PR**, which auto-merges after CI — so the
> see-it-fail fixture is the only gate a converted check gets there. Convert only what you can prove;
> anything shakier stays prose and waits for the weekly sweep's reviewed PR.

1. **Author the check** in the owning pack, at the ladder's highest check rung the rule allows: an entry
   in `<pack>/declared-checks.json` when its logic is patterns over files, dropping to `<pack>/<rule>.mjs`
   listed in `pack.mjs` only when it needs what patterns can't say. Either way the failure message *is*
   the rule (what / why / fix — plus, for a rule module, the `doc:` pointer back to the prose; a
   declaration carries no pointer and must state its own case).
2. **Write the fixture first and see it fail** — a violating fixture must find, a clean one must
   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
   doesn't ship.
3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory when the rule is
   directional by kind, or when the condition is blocking-grade but **irreversible by the time it is
   observable** (an append-only transcript, a published artifact). A blocking finding no edit can
   retract never converges — it spends every remaining Stop cycle on something nothing can fix.
   Advisory there is *diagnostic*: it names the cause the moment it appears.
   - **Declare `since: '<today>'` beside the severity.** A blocking check is enforced as advisory for
     its first two weeks, so a conversion whose backlog the tree still carries lands at its real
     severity now and starts biting once somebody has had time to clear it. Never soften a real
     defect to `advisory` for that reason — the window is what makes softening unnecessary.
   - **Prefer a positive allowlist over an enumerated list of the bad cases.** Match the one allowed
     shape and flag everything else, rather than banning the violations you can name. An allowlist
     catches a variant that doesn't exist yet the day it lands, and turns an indirection (a value
     passed through a variable instead of written literally) into a finding too — refusing to reason
     about indirection is the feature. Invert only where the allowed set is genuinely open-ended.
4. **Delete the prose the check now covers** — whole, never trimmed. The deletion test below is
   how you decide which paragraphs those are.

**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's
*own* header list, not elsewhere in the template.) Parse only as much as you need, and hold the
check to the same fixture bar.

**When a rule mandates a *form*, the check asserts that form — never the intent behind it.** Where
the prose says *write it exactly like this*, the check's whole job is deciding whether the artifact
is that form; inferring what the author meant is unbounded in the wrong direction and leaves the
likeliest reproduction uncaught, since a hand-picked marker list always misses the phrasing nobody
enumerated. Expect a form check to fire on something that breaks the form while causing no harm —
that's the rule as written doing its job, not a reason to re-add intent-guessing.

When even a scoped parser can't make detection confident, **leave the prose and log the
candidate** to a tagged conversion-backlog issue rather than shipping a shaky check.

## Coming out: the deletion test

Coming out of a conversion, apply the **deletion test**: prose a mechanism fully covers is
deleted, never trimmed. Ask it of every paragraph standing beside a landed check — *with this
paragraph gone, would the check still catch every violation it describes **and** tell the agent
how to fix it?* If yes, it is redundant: delete it whole. The check's failure message is where
the rule lives now and its header comment is where the rationale lives, so a paragraph restating
either pays twice and is the drift trap waiting to spring.

Before concluding prose is the only carrier, look at the pack's **skills** too — an
activity-scoped skill often already holds the map a rule is repeating. Keep only what no artifact
carries.

The test **discriminates** rather than just deleting: a paragraph stays whole whenever it carries
something the check does not — a second rule in the same breath, an exemption the check can't
encode, a value the check can't judge, or a remedy the finding's own `fix` line never states
(a finding renders `what` / `why` / `fix` / `doc`, never the rule's `description`, so a remedy
that lives only in the description is not carried). Two worked calls: an `npm test` invariant
went entirely — the check caught it and the testing-guide skill already listed the suites —
while an `extension-test/` mirror bullet stayed, because the check beside it enforced only the
`package.json` list's sync with the tree and never the mirror convention itself.

Whether a check covers a rule is a judgment about meaning, so this test is applied by a
**reader**, not mechanized.

## Bounds

- **One PR, bounded surface** — the new rule module, its `pack.mjs` line, its fixture, and the
  trimmed prose. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there.
- **Never delete a rule you didn't convert** — the deletion test is only ever asked of a rule a
  *landed* check now enforces.
- Run the suite and the sweep green before the PR goes up, and never push to `main` directly. The
  sweep opens its own PR for the owner's approval; the upgrade pass adds its conversion to the
  growth-extract PR already being opened, and opens none of its own.

1	# shepherd — this repo's own rules
2	
3	The capture surface for lessons **specific to this repository**. Loaded into every session
4	through the rules index, so what lands here should be a directive an agent can act on, not a
5	description of how something works.
6	
7	A lesson that would hold in another repo does not belong here — propose it to the Claudinite
8	canon instead, where every repo gets it.
9	
10	- **Reading this fleet's activity to rank or report it** — filter Claudinite's own artifacts out
11	  of **every** stream you collect, not just the first one you thought of. The machine is the
12	  busiest actor in this fleet, and its bookkeeping does not merely appear in a size-or-discussion
13	  ranking, it wins it: a dispatch issue collects a comment per executor stage, so it outweighs the
14	  work it dispatched, and a guard written for pull requests while issues go through unfiltered
15	  leaves the whole hole open. Recognize a machine artifact with the engine's own `isDispatchTitle`
16	  rather than a private regex, since the dispatch-title format is the scheduler's to change. Count
17	  the maintenance total where it is **tallied**, never by dropping items in the fetch: an issue the
18	  machinery filed and closed is still a true account of how much of the day this fleet spent
19	  servicing itself.
20	
21	- **Carrying an artifact directory over from a repo being retired** (the Sheepdog → Shepherd
22	  fleet-enforcer handoff) — verify the *machinery that produces it* came over too, not just its
23	  historical output. `digests/`'s files landed in #23 and read as fully carried; the missing
24	  generator (Sheepdog's `sheepdog-local` pack and its `fleet-digest` task) surfaced only later, in
25	  #27, once checked separately from the output. A copied output folder visually launders the
26	  absence of its live producer — audit for the generator explicitly, in the same pass, rather than
27	  inferring it from the presence of past output.
28	
29	- **Dropping a folded/aggregate `GENERATED` file because "the next run recomputes it"** — check
30	  first whether the recompute's own *inputs* retain the same history the current output does. A
31	  stateless recompute over inputs each fleet member keeps only for a bounded window starts the
32	  series shorter than a file carried over from elsewhere already holds — nearly true of
33	  `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json`, first left out of the Sheepdog carryover (#23) on exactly that
34	  assumption, then copied over verbatim once the gap was caught (#31). "The generator will refill
35	  it" is not sufficient on its own; confirm the generator's inputs cover the same span first.
36	
37	- **Scoping a fleet-wide text/reference sweep from this repo** — don't trust
38	  `mcp__github__search_code` alone to enumerate the affected member repos; its index can lag and
39	  silently undercount. Cross-check against the full known member roster (fetch each member's
40	  `.claudinite-checks.json` directly) before scoping the sweep: a Sheepdog-reference sweep found
41	  only 3 repos via search but 11 by direct check (#24).
42	
43	- **Waiting on this repo's PR CI** — it's a single `checks` job that completes in roughly 7–15
44	  seconds (measured directly across #30, #32, #59, #67). Poll `pull_request_read get_check_runs`
45	  in a short loop instead of a fixed or backgrounded `sleep`, and don't call
46	  `enable_pr_auto_merge` in the same breath as opening the PR — GitHub refuses it with "unstable
47	  status" if the check hasn't started yet, which is a sign to wait and re-poll, not license to
48	  merge by hand instead (#59). Before stating a PR's status in a closing callout, read
49	  `get_check_runs` rather than asserting "CI running" as an unread guess (#30), and skip grepping
50	  `.github/workflows/*.yml` to guess whether a workflow gates the merge — the check runs already
51	  say so directly (#60).
52	
53	- **Firing an `AskUserQuestion`** — check first whether the answer is already decided: by a rule
54	  already loaded in context, by fleet or repo state one read away (a sibling's
55	  `.claudinite-checks.json`, a pending adoption interview), or by the option marked
56	  "(Recommended)" simply being the status quo. Batch every open decision a run will need into one
57	  question instead of asking serially. Four sessions lost 17 to 105 minutes of pure
58	  human-round-trip idle time to questions whose answer was already available or was the presented
59	  default (#2, #22, #28, #32).
60	
61	- **Leaving multiple PRs open for the owner after a fleet-wide sweep** — call
62	  `subscribe_pr_activity` on every one of them, not a sample. #24's sweep subscribed only 2 of 12
63	  open PRs, then spent over two hours and ~29 API calls re-polling the other 10 on a self-armed
64	  hourly wake-up with zero state change, while the 2 subscribed PRs' merges arrived instantly as
65	  activity events the moment the owner acted.
66	
67	- **Triaging a `fleet-drift` issue that names another repo** — don't spend a call on
68	  `mcp__github__get_file_contents` (or any other repo-scoped MCP read) against that repo: this
69	  session's GitHub access is scoped to `missingbulb/Shepherd` only, and every such repo-scoped
70	  call is denied outright. A tool that takes no repo argument — `search_code`, `search_issues` —
71	  is not scoped the same way and can still return results from other repos, so it isn't a safe
72	  substitute either; only the repo-scoped reads are guaranteed to refuse. Five separate triage
73	  subagents each independently spent a call rediscovering the repo-scoped denial before falling
74	  back to the only place the answer actually lives — the issue body's own self-description of how
75	  the item converges (#104).
76	
77	- **Hunting for this repo's own standing tracker issue by its exact title** —
78	  `mcp__github__search_issues` doesn't reliably narrow to an exact title even quoted: it runs
79	  natural-language matching over the whole issue corpus, so a quoted title can come back as one hit
80	  buried among dozens of unrelated ones (confirmed live: a quoted exact title returned 30 of 180
81	  issues, nearly all unrelated, with the real match merely first by relevance).
82	  `mcp__github__list_issues` carries no free-text query parameter at all — it filters only
83	  structurally, by `labels`/`state`/`field_filters`/`since` — so hunting a title through it means
84	  filtering by label/state first and scanning the returned titles yourself, never passing the title
85	  as a query string. Neither tool takes a `minimal_output` flag; shrink the response with the
86	  `fields` param instead, listing only the fields you need (#104, #88, #209, #210).
87	
88	- **Pushing a change that touches `.github/workflows/`, `.claudinite-checks.json`, or pack
89	  config** — run `node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` locally first. It's
90	  the exact script the PR's `checks` CI job runs, and finding a `[BLOCKING]` finding live on the PR
91	  costs a full push-PR-CI-diagnose-fix-re-push round trip that one ~4-second local run skips
92	  (#106).
93	
94	- **Dispatching concurrent subagents that each `git show` a file into the shared scratchpad** (the
95	  conversation-extract fan-out, or any similar parallel mining pattern) — give every dispatch a
96	  unique output filename. A shared generic name (`log.jsonl`) collides across concurrent downloads
97	  and silently hands one agent another agent's bytes; this exact contamination hit a prior
98	  growth-extract run in six or more of its own subagents (#73) and recurred in this run's own
99	  fan-out before being caught and re-fetched to a uniquely-named path.
100	
101	- **Branching off this checkout's local `main`** — it does not track the live default branch, and
102	  has been observed pinned at the repo's very first commit. A plain `git checkout -b <name> main`
103	  silently branches from that frozen history and the next script that expects current content
104	  (e.g. a `.claudinite/` path) fails confusingly. Always `git fetch origin main` and branch from
105	  `origin/main` explicitly (#73).
106
